title: Gateways, registry and governance
summary: As servers and agents multiply, put policy in a gateway (API Management), curated bundles behind one endpoint (Foundry Toolbox) and a catalog with an approval workflow (a private registry) instead of wiring every agent to every server.
useIf: Several teams publish or consume MCP servers and you need central auth, limits, audit, versioning and discovery.
avoidIf: One agent uses two servers you own. Direct connection with allowed tools and approvals is simpler.

explain.md: **API Management (APIM)** can expose a managed REST API as an MCP server (operations become tools) or front an existing MCP server. Policies such as rate limiting, quota, IP filtering, caching and tracing currently apply to all tools in a server. It supports MCP tools only, not resources or prompts, and is not supported in workspaces. Inbound auth is a subscription key in `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` or Entra tokens checked with `validate-azure-ad-token`. Outbound credentials use the credential manager and `get-authorization-context` [[r17]] [[r36]].

**Foundry Toolbox** is a versioned, governed bundle of tools (MCP, A2A, OpenAPI, Azure AI Search, web search and more) exposed as one MCP-compatible endpoint, `.../toolboxes/{name}/versions/{version}/mcp`. It adds central Entra auth, OAuth passthrough (Foundry's feature name, so check it against the token rules in [[r5]]), guardrails and promotion of a default version without redeploying agents. Tool search and skills are Preview as of 2026-10-13, as are long-running calls through MCP tasks. A first OAuth use can return `CONSENT_REQUIRED` (`-32006`) [[r16]].

For one agent, Foundry's MCP tool takes `server_url`, `server_label`, `allowed_tools`, `require_approval` and `project_connection_id`. Approvals arrive as `mcp_approval_request` items answered with `mcp_approval_response`. Non-streaming calls time out at 100 seconds, and private MCP needs Standard Agent Setup with private networking [[r15]].

**Registries.** The official MCP Registry is Preview: it stores `server.json` metadata, uses reverse-DNS names with namespace verification, holds no private servers, is not designed for self-hosting, and host apps should consume downstream registries instead of calling it directly [[r10]]. Azure API Center keeps a private inventory of remote or local servers and links to Foundry tool catalogs [[tr15]].

pitfalls.symptom: Resources and prompts disappear behind the gateway
pitfalls.cause: API Management currently supports MCP tools only
pitfalls.fix: Use direct access for those primitives or pick a gateway that carries them

pitfalls.symptom: Production breaks when a registry resets
pitfalls.cause: The Preview public registry was a runtime dependency
pitfalls.fix: Mirror approved entries into a private registry and pin them

pitfalls.cause: A toolbox tool needs the user's OAuth consent before first use
pitfalls.fix: Handle `-32006` in the client and guide the user through consent

scenarios.title: Twenty teams, tools only, mixed frameworks
scenarios.situation: Twenty teams publish MCP servers that expose tools only. Agents run on several frameworks, not only Foundry. Security wants quotas, rate limits and Entra validation in one place.
scenarios.question: Where do you put governance?

options.name: An API Management gateway with API Center registration
options.why: Policies apply across tools, auth is central and registration gives discovery for any framework.
options.tradeoff: A new hop, and no resources or prompts.

options.name: A Foundry Toolbox per domain
options.tradeoff: Managed in Foundry, although any MCP client can use it, and key features such as tool search are Preview.

options.name: Each agent connects directly to each server
options.why: Credentials, limits and audit are duplicated twenty times.

flips.if: Servers must expose prompts or resources
flips.then: Connect directly or use another gateway.

flips.if: You need versioned bundles with default-version promotion

scenarios.takeaway: Put policy where every path crosses it.

scenarios.title: Foundry agents sharing a toolset
scenarios.situation: A Foundry team runs many agents that need the same CRM, search and ticket tools. They want to promote a new tool version to every agent without redeploying.
unknowns: Is Preview tool search acceptable here?
Which auth model does each tool use?
scenarios.question: How should the tools be packaged?

options.name: A Foundry Toolbox with a promoted default version
options.why: One endpoint, central auth and version promotion without agent redeploys.
options.tradeoff: Managed in Foundry and some features are Preview.

options.name: Per-agent MCP tool configs with `allowed_tools`
options.tradeoff: Duplicated config and credentials, and every agent must change together.

options.name: Pin the public registry entry and call it from each agent
options.why: The public registry is Preview and not meant for host apps to call directly.
options.tradeoff: Use it only to discover servers.

flips.if: Only one agent uses the tools
flips.then: A direct MCP tool is enough.

flips.if: Preview status is unacceptable for production
flips.then: Use the stable parts only and gate Preview features.

scenarios.takeaway: Bundles pay off when many agents share one versioned toolset.

scenarios.title: A small team with two servers
scenarios.situation: A small team ships one agent that uses two MCP servers it operates. It needs approvals for risky calls and wants to ship this month.
scenarios.question: How much governance do you add?

options.name: Direct MCP tool with `allowed_tools`, `require_approval` and pinned versions
options.why: Gives control where risk is, with no extra layer to build or run.
options.tradeoff: No central quotas or audit until the estate grows.

options.name: Front both servers with a gateway
options.tradeoff: Extra setup that a two-server team may not need yet.

options.name: Build a private registry and approval portal first
options.why: It delays delivery for a catalog of two entries.
options.tradeoff: Right when dozens of servers and teams exist.

flips.then: Add a gateway and a registry.

flips.if: Risky calls multiply beyond what reviewers can approve one by one
flips.then: Add policy-based approvals and central audit through a gateway.

scenarios.takeaway: Match governance to the size of the estate.

Versioned tool bundle behind one MCP-compatible endpoint

quiz.explain: These roles come from the API Management, Toolbox, API Center and registry documentation. The registry is Preview and public only, and host apps should use downstream registries.

quiz.q: Your consumers need MCP prompts and resources. Which statement about API Management is correct?
options: It carries prompts and resources automatically
It currently supports MCP tools but not resources or prompts
It works inside workspaces for MCP servers
It replaces OAuth in the MCP spec
quiz.explain: API Management currently supports MCP server tools, not resources or prompts, and MCP capabilities are not supported in workspaces. It does not replace OAuth.

flashcards.front: What does API Management support for MCP today?
flashcards.back: Tools only, with policies for all tools in a server (rate limit, quota, IP filter, caching, tracing). No resources, prompts or workspaces.
A versioned, governed tool bundle served from one MCP-compatible endpoint, with central auth and default-version promotion. Tool search and skills are Preview.

flashcards.front: Why not depend on the public MCP Registry at runtime?
flashcards.back: It is Preview, can reset data, holds public servers only, and host apps should consume downstream registries instead.
